text: Right now we're tracking a Russian satellite that has taken some very hostile moves near a U.S. registered satellite that provides radar data supporting Ukraine. We're watching right now to see what this Russian satellite does next. Does it take some action to disable or destroy the ICEYE satellite? Does it try to interfere with it in some way? Or does it simply move on to another orbit? It has moved itself into a position where with very little energy expenditure and maneuvering it can get very close to the commercial satellite and probably do something that it's not

supposed to do. It could have a jammer on it. It could try to jam a signal coming to or from that ICEYE satellite. It could have a laser on it. It could try to damage equipment on that ICEYE satellite. It could try to blind a sensor on that ICEYE satellite. It could have a kinetic weapon. It could have a projectile that's meant to shoot at the ICEYE satellite. So if you think about all these different things that could happen some of them are just trying to prove a point. I can do this and you can't stop me. On the other end it could permanently damage or destroy

that commercial satellite and we don't know what Russia is intending so we can't really say which of these things are more probable or likely right now. We have seen Russia place its satellites in these highly alerting orbits with other U.S. satellites but we haven't seen a weapon used or tested in those scenarios. But when you pair all of these circumstantial data points with what we see Russia doing on Earth that's when we really should be concerned. Hybrid warfare, gray zone warfare that we see in Europe, a suspected Russian plot for a drone attack in Germany,

cyber attacks, jamming and spoofing of GPS signals, a lot of things the Russians are doing to push boundaries on Earth. We shouldn't be surprised if they try to do something like that in space right now. From a policy making standpoint there's really two types of issues we want to think about. One, what is normal? What is not normal? What is hostile? What is escalatory in space? Can we get a sense of where that line is? Right now we don't really have a line. We can't say because of this rule that satellite is too close. Because of this rule that satellite shouldn't be co-planar with

my satellite. There's nothing like that right now. Secondly we have to think about times when maybe Russia's going to do something that is crossing the line. It's going to take an action where it wants to challenge a rule. It wants to challenge a norm. It wants to push the boundaries. How would we respond to that? And that whole process that feeds into this notion of deterrence and that these actions you take they have consequences.
